The proposed legislation has long been opposed by New Jersey's Roman Catholic Church

The measure would also allow victims to sue any liable institution

Feb. 14, 2019

New Jersey Gov. Phil Murphy on Thursday threw his support behind proposed legislation that would expand the statute of limitations in civil cases for sexual-assault victims, a measure long opposed by the state’s Roman Catholic Church.

The bill would create a one-time, two-year window for pursuing legal action for anyone previously barred from filing a civil complaint. The proposed legislation would give them the right to bring litigation between Dec. 1, 2019 and Nov. 30, 2021.

The current statute of limitations for civil cases is two years, but because victims sometimes suppress their memories of such incidents for years or don’t connect their psychological injuries to the abuse, the legislation proposes a much longer period for filing complaints.

The measure also would allow child victims to bring civil cases until the age of 55 or seven years from the time they become aware of the injury, whichever is later. Adult victims would have a seven-year time frame to pursue civil actions from the time of the incident or seven years after they become aware of the abuse.

There is no statute of limitations for criminal cases of sexual assault in New Jersey.

The proposed bill also would allow victims to sue any liable institution.

“Victims of sexual abuse, especially those victimized in childhood, deserve to find doors held open for them as they seek justice against their abusers,” Gov. Murphy, a Democrat, said.

Advocates for sexual-abuse victims have been calling for a change in New Jersey law for several years, but the matter has taken on new urgency following the release in August of a grand-jury report detailing the alleged molestation of over 1,000 children by more than 300 priests in Pennsylvania.

“The Catholic Bishops of New Jersey are committed to keeping our teaching, worship and ministry spaces safe for everyone, especially children,” said Patrick Brannigan, executive director of the New Jersey Catholic Conference, which represents the state’s Catholic bishops. “All of our dioceses have committed to assisting victims of abuse whenever and however we can.”

Mr. Brannigan said the New Jersey Catholic Conference supports the elimination of the statute of limitations for future crimes for both perpetrators and institutions. The conference also backs eliminating the statute of limitations for prior offenses for perpetrators only.

Catholic Church officials in New Jersey said last fall they would set up a compensation fund for victims of sexual abuse by clergy whose financial claims are legally barred by the statute of limitations. The church officials appointed Kenneth Feinberg and Camille Biros, who also administered compensation funds for Pennsylvania State University sexual-abuse victims and victims of the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, to manage the fund.

The compensation fund has a “significantly lower level of proof and corroboration than required in a court of law,” Mr. Brannigan said.

New Jersey’s Catholic Church established the compensation fund after the New Jersey attorney general said he was forming a task force to investigate sexual-assault allegations made against the church.

And on Wednesday, the five Catholic dioceses in New Jersey released the names of 189 clergy members that have been credibly accused of sexually abusing minors. All the named clerics had either left the church or died.

In New York, Gov. Andrew Cuomo signed similar legislation on Thursday expanding the statute of limitations for civil and criminal actions involving the sexual abuse of minors.

Assemblywoman Annette Quijano and state Sen. Joseph Vitale, both Democrats, are sponsoring the New Jersey bill. The state Senate Judiciary Committee will hold a public hearing on the legislation on March 7.

“Not one more victim should be turned away and denied their day in court,” said Mr. Vitale, who has pushed for the bill for over a decade.

New Jersey’s state Senate President Steve Sweeney, a Democrat, also supports the legislation, according to a state Senate staffer.
